dialogues.title: The Job Interview
dialogues.scene: A candidate meets a hiring manager and answers common interview questions.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.target: Good morning. Thanks for coming in. Please have a seat.
lines.ref: A polite, formal welcome. 'Have a seat' = sit down.

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.target: Good morning. Thank you for the opportunity.
lines.ref: A courteous reply that shows appreciation.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.target: Could you tell me a little about yourself?
lines.ref: A classic opening question; keep the answer short and relevant.

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.target: Of course. I'm a graphic designer with five years of experience.
lines.ref: State your role and how long you've done it.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.target: Why do you want to work for our company?
lines.ref: They want to hear that you know and like the company.

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.target: I admire your work, and I believe I can contribute a lot.
lines.ref: A positive, confident answer.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.target: What would you say is your greatest strength?
lines.ref: 'greatest strength' = your best quality.

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.target: I'm very organized, and I always meet my deadlines.
lines.ref: Give a strength with a concrete result.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.target: Great. Do you have any questions for me?
lines.ref: Always prepare one or two questions to ask.

lines.speaker: Candidate
lines.target: Yes, what does a typical day in this role look like?
lines.ref: A smart question showing genuine interest.

dialogues.note: In English-speaking interviews, arriving 10 minutes early and giving a firm handshake are seen as signs of professionalism and respect.

dialogues.title: Checking Into a Hotel
dialogues.scene: A guest arrives at the front desk to check in and reports a problem.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.target: Good evening. Welcome to the Grand Hotel. How can I help you?
lines.ref: A standard, friendly hotel greeting.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Hi, I have a reservation under the name Carter.
lines.ref: 'under the name' = booked in the name of.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.target: Let me check. Yes, a double room for three nights.
lines.ref: Confirming the booking details.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: That's right. Does the room have wifi?
lines.ref: Asking about a facility.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.target: Yes, it's free. Here is your key card. Room 204.
lines.ref: 'key card' = the card that opens the door.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Thank you. What time is breakfast served?
lines.ref: 'is served' is a passive form for scheduled service.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.target: Breakfast is from seven to ten in the restaurant.
lines.ref: Giving the meal times.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Excuse me, the air conditioning in my room isn't working.
lines.ref: Politely reporting a problem with the room.

lines.speaker: Receptionist
lines.target: I'm very sorry. I'll send someone up right away.
lines.ref: 'right away' = immediately; 'I'll' is a spontaneous offer.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Thank you, I appreciate it.
lines.ref: A polite way to thank someone for their help.

dialogues.note: Tipping the porter who carries your bags a small amount is customary in many English-speaking countries, especially the United States.

dialogues.title: Making Plans With a Friend
dialogues.scene: Two friends decide what to do at the weekend and agree on a time.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.target: Hey, are you free this weekend?
lines.ref: 'are you free' = do you have time available.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: I think so. What did you have in mind?
lines.ref: 'have in mind' = are thinking of.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.target: How about going to the new art exhibition?
lines.ref: 'How about + -ing' is a common way to suggest.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Hmm, to be honest, museums aren't really my thing.
lines.ref: 'not my thing' = something I don't enjoy.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.target: Fair enough. We could go hiking instead.
lines.ref: 'Fair enough' accepts the point; 'instead' offers an alternative.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Now that sounds great! I've been wanting to get outdoors.
lines.ref: 'sounds great' shows enthusiasm; note the present perfect continuous.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.target: Perfect. Shall we meet at the trailhead around nine?
lines.ref: 'Shall we' proposes; 'around nine' = approximately 9:00.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Nine works for me. Should I bring some snacks?
lines.ref: 'works for me' = that time suits me.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.target: Good idea. I'll bring water and a map.
lines.ref: Dividing up who brings what.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.target: Great, see you on Saturday then!
lines.ref: Confirming the day before parting.

dialogues.note: Suggestions in English are often softened with 'How about...?' or 'Shall we...?' rather than direct commands, which can sound bossy among friends.

dialogues.title: A Formal Meeting
dialogues.scene: Colleagues present an idea, ask for clarification, and agree on next steps.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.target: Thanks for joining. Today we'll discuss the new marketing plan.
lines.ref: Opening a meeting and stating its topic.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.target: I'd like to propose that we focus on social media first.
lines.ref: 'I'd like to propose' is a formal way to suggest.

lines.speaker: David
lines.target: Could you clarify what you mean by 'focus'?
lines.ref: 'clarify' = explain more clearly.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.target: Certainly. I mean we should spend most of our budget there.
lines.ref: 'Certainly' politely agrees to explain.

lines.speaker: David
lines.target: I see your point, but I'm not sure it's enough.
lines.ref: 'I see your point' acknowledges before disagreeing politely.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.target: That's a valid concern. What would you suggest instead?
lines.ref: Inviting an alternative view.

lines.speaker: David
lines.target: Perhaps we could combine it with email campaigns.
lines.ref: 'Perhaps we could' is a tentative, polite suggestion.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.target: That makes sense. I'm happy to work on both.
lines.ref: 'That makes sense' shows agreement.

lines.speaker: Chair
lines.target: Great. Let's agree on that and review the results next month.
lines.ref: Summarizing the decision and next step.

lines.speaker: David
lines.target: Sounds good. I'll send a summary by email.
lines.ref: Confirming a follow-up action.

dialogues.note: In professional English, disagreement is usually cushioned: phrases like 'I see your point, but...' keep the tone respectful and collaborative.

dialogues.title: At the Pharmacy
dialogues.scene: A customer describes symptoms and asks about medication and instructions.

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.target: Hello, how can I help you today?
lines.ref: A standard, welcoming opener.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.target: Hi, I've had a sore throat and a headache since yesterday.
lines.ref: Present perfect + 'since' describes symptoms continuing to now.

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.target: I'm sorry to hear that. Do you have a fever?
lines.ref: 'I'm sorry to hear that' shows sympathy.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.target: A slight one. Is there something you'd recommend?
lines.ref: 'would recommend' asks for a professional suggestion.

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.target: You could take these tablets. They should ease the pain.
lines.ref: 'could' and 'should' soften advice and prediction.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.target: How often should I take them?
lines.ref: Asking about dosage frequency.

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.target: Take one every eight hours, with food.
lines.ref: Giving clear dosage instructions.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.target: Are there any side effects I should know about?
lines.ref: 'side effects' = unwanted reactions to medicine.

lines.speaker: Pharmacist
lines.target: They may make you drowsy, so avoid driving.
lines.ref: 'drowsy' = sleepy; 'avoid + -ing' gives a warning.

lines.speaker: Customer
lines.target: Understood. Thank you for your help.
lines.ref: Confirming understanding and thanking.

dialogues.note: In many English-speaking countries, pharmacists can give advice on minor illnesses for free, so people often ask them before booking a doctor.

dialogues.title: Dinner With a Friend's Family
dialogues.scene: A guest makes small talk, compliments the host, and offers to help.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.target: Welcome! We're so glad you could make it.
lines.ref: 'make it' = manage to come; a warm welcome.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Thank you for having me. Your home is lovely.
lines.ref: 'Thank you for having me' is the standard guest phrase.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.target: That's kind of you. Please, make yourself at home.
lines.ref: 'make yourself at home' = relax and feel comfortable.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Something smells amazing. What are you cooking?
lines.ref: A natural compliment that starts small talk.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.target: It's a roast. I hope you're hungry!
lines.ref: 'a roast' is a traditional cooked meal.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Absolutely. Is there anything I can do to help?
lines.ref: Politely offering to help before the meal.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.target: You could set the table if you don't mind.
lines.ref: 'if you don't mind' softens the request.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: Not at all. Where do you keep the plates?
lines.ref: 'Not at all' happily accepts; asking where things are.

lines.speaker: Host
lines.target: In the cupboard on the left. Thanks so much.
lines.ref: Giving directions and thanking.

lines.speaker: Guest
lines.target: This meal was delicious. Thank you for a wonderful evening.
lines.ref: A warm compliment and thanks as the evening ends.

vocab: to make it (to manage to come)
to make yourself at home (to relax as a guest)
to set the table (to lay out plates and cutlery)
dialogues.note: Bringing a small gift such as wine, flowers, or a dessert when invited to dinner is a common courtesy in most English-speaking cultures.
